subtype: Approach: check registration with the regulator before paying [Action]
passage: Nour had saved for two years in a café job in Rotterdam, and a colleague's cousin recommended an online platform and an adviser with a slick brochure. Before sending anything, Nour sat with the laptop and Chen, a flatmate, at the kitchen table. "First step," Nour said, "find the public register of the national financial regulator." They typed the platform's name. No match. They typed the adviser's name. Nothing again. Chen searched for reviews and found a string of complaints about withdrawals not arriving. It took twelve minutes. "Convincing brochure, though," Chen said. Nour closed the laptop and said, "That was cheaper than finding out the hard way." The brochure went into the recycling.

qa.q: How long did the checking take?
What did Nour feel about closing the laptop and the brochure?
qa.a: Nour felt relieved at not having lost money, since the checking was cheaper than finding out the hard way.

qa.q: What could Nour do next if still wanting to invest, and why?
qa.a: Nour could talk to a licensed adviser found on the official register, because a registered person can be held to rules.

qa.q: How might Chen see Nour's plan to check before paying?
qa.a: Chen seems glad to help and impressed that a persuasive pitch did not win.

grounding: Before sending money a person checks whether the platform and adviser are on the regulator's register and reads complaints.

subtype: Approach: check registration with the regulator before paying [Action]
passage:
In the office pantry, Chinmay showed Sabina the ad on his phone: an adviser with a smiling photo, 'registered expert', promising 'expert picks, ₹4,999 for three months'. 'He's got thousands of followers,' Chinmay said. 'I'm signing up tonight. Join me?'
Sabina said she'd check first, and went back to her desk. It took about twelve minutes. First, she opened the securities regulator's official website and searched its list of registered investment advisers for the name. Nothing. Second, she searched the registration number printed in the ad. It belonged to a different person, in another city. Third, she typed the adviser's name with the word 'complaint'. Pages of people saying they'd paid and been blocked.
She walked back to the pantry and put her phone next to his. Chinmay read for a while. 'The photo looked so real.'
He didn't sign up that night.

qa.q: Why did Sabina say she'd check first?
qa.a: She was cautious and a little wary of a pitch built on followers and a photo, and wanted facts before trust.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's checks mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Searching the regulator's official list, since a real registered adviser would be on it; the mismatched registration number confirmed the ad was false.

qa.q: How does the ad look to Chinmay after reading the complaints?
qa.a: Chinmay is shaken that the photo looked so real, and sees that followers are no proof of honesty.

grounding: Shows a person checking the regulator's register and complaints before paying an adviser, replacing trust in a persuasive pitch.

passage:
Subject: about the trading app link you sent

Hi Seema,
Thank you for thinking of me. I know you only sent it because your friend made money. But before paying the ₹10,000 joining amount, I did what my professor told us to do with any money offer, and I want to show you what I found.
First, I looked up the platform on the securities regulator's official website, in its list of registered intermediaries. It isn't there. Then I checked the 'adviser' on the same site. Not registered either. Then I searched the app's name with 'withdrawal problem'. Dozens of complaints, all saying the same thing: easy deposits, then fees to take money out.
All of this took me less than fifteen minutes. Please don't put in any more, and if you already have, the bank and the cybercrime helpline can help. I'll come with you if you like.
Love,
Sudha

qa.q: How much was the joining amount?
What might Sudha be worried about in writing to Seema?
qa.a: Sudha is worried that Seema may already have put money in, and cares enough to offer to go to the bank together.

qa.q: What could Seema do if money has already gone in?
qa.a: Stop paying, save the chats and screenshots, and report to the bank and the cybercrime helpline, with Sudha or another trusted adult alongside.

qa.q: How might Seema feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed or defensive at first, but also cared for, since Sudha offers thanks and help instead of blame.

grounding: Shows a person checking a platform and adviser against the regulator's register and reading complaints before sending any money.
